title: Eyelid Malpositions: Ptosis & Entropion Clinical Mastery
summary: A comprehensive guide to the evaluation and surgical management of blepharoptosis and entropion, emphasizing clinical examination techniques, ocular protective mechanisms, and levator-based surgical interventions.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Blepharoptosis (Ptosis) is the abnormally low position of the upper eyelid margin in primary gaze. Entropion is the inward turning of the eyelid margin towards the globe, potentially causing trichiasis and corneal scarring.

sections.title: The Comprehensive Ptosis Exam (Right Eye Focus)

rows: Distance from pupillary light reflex to upper lid margin
Distance from pupillary light reflex to lower lid margin
Vertical distance between upper and lower lid margins
Excursion of lid from extreme downgaze to upgaze (negating frontalis)
Distance from lid margin to the skin crease

sections.title: Red Flags in Ptosis
content: New-onset Ptosis + Pupil Involvement (R/O Aneurysm/CN III)
Ptosis + Miosis + Anhydrosis (Horner Syndrome - R/O Carotid Dissection/Pancoast)
Variability/Fatigability (R/O Myasthenia Gravis)
Proptosis + Ptosis (R/O Orbital mass)
Poor Bell's Phenomenon (High risk for exposure keratopathy post-op)

sections.title: Entropion: Clinical Evaluation
content: Snap-back Test: Pull lid down; slow return without blink indicates laxity.
Distraction Test: Pull lid away from globe; >10mm indicates horizontal laxity.
White Line Sign: Visualization of disinserted lower lid retractors through conjunctiva.
Orbicularis Overriding: Eyelid margin rotates inward upon forceful lid closure.
Cicatricial Check: Eversion of lid to look for tarsal scarring or symblepharon.

sections.title: Management of Involutional Entropion
content: 1. Horizontal Lid Shortening (Lateral Tarsal Strip)
2. Retractor Reattachment (Jones/Jones-Wies procedure)
3. Everting Sutures (Quickert sutures for temporary/spastic)
4. Transverse Tarsotomy (Wies procedure for cicatricial components)

sections.title: Surgery: Levator Resection (For Good LF)
content: 1. Skin Incision: Mark the desired lid crease and incise through skin and orbicularis.
2. Orbital Septum Entry: Open the septum to expose pre-aponeurotic fat pads.
3. Levator Identification: Identify the white, glistening levator aponeurosis beneath fat.
4. Dissection: Free levator from underlying Muller's muscle and conjunctiva (optional) or tarsus.
5. Resection: Measure the amount of levator to be excised based on ptosis severity.
6. Suture Attachment: Fixate the shortened levator to the upper third of the tarsal plate.
7. Intraoperative Adjustment: Check lid height and contour with patient sitting upright (if local).
8. Skin Closure: Incorporate levator fibers into skin sutures to reform the lid crease.

content.explanation: High Effort Results In Negative Gains for the 'normal' lid. Lifting the more ptotic lid may cause the contralateral lid to drop due to decreased equal innervation (Law of Equal Innervation).

rows: Massage, suture release, or spacer graft

sections.title: Clinical Pearls: Ptosis & Entropion
content: Always perform a Phenylephrine test to assess Muller muscle contribution.
Check for Lagophthalmos pre-operatively to avoid post-op corneal disasters.
Congenital ptosis often shows lid lag in downgaze; involutional ptosis does not.
In entropion, check for symblepharon to rule out Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid (OCP) before surgery.
The 'Lid Distraction' test is the gold standard for measuring horizontal laxity.

sections.title: Common Surgical Dosages & Tools
content: Local: Lidocaine 2% with Epinephrine 1:100,000 (minimizes bleeding).
Sutures: 5-0 or 6-0 Vicryl for levator-tarsal fixation; 6-0 Prolene or Silk for skin.
Instruments: Desmarres lid retractor, Westcott scissors, Bishop-Harmon forceps.
Hemostasis: Bipolar cautery is essential to avoid thermal damage to the levator.
